extracted.intended_audience: aspiring storytellers and general literate readers of The Spectator
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for composing short narratives and illustrative fables that command attention — emphasizing surprise, moral purpose, stylistic grace, and truthful depiction of human nature. Geared toward writers aiming to please and instruct an 18th-century reading public.

rubrics_metrics.name: Surprise as the life of stories
rubrics_metrics.description: "Surprize is so much the Life of Stories, that every one aims at it, who endeavours to please by telling them."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Aim for a "turn of surprize" in a story — it produces attention and success; however, surprise is a double-edged tool: while it makes some characters and stories famed, when misapplied it has been the ruin of others. Use surprise deliberately and compatibly with character and plausibility.

rubrics_metrics.name: Style as beautifying graces
rubrics_metrics.description: "Smooth Delivery, an elegant Choice of Words, and a sweet Arrangement, are all beautifying Graces."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Polish diction, rhythm, and ordering of material to beautify a narrative. Treat these as important surface virtues, but not as substitutes for the particular incidents and emotional effects that truly command an audience's attention.

rubrics_metrics.name: Particulars that command attention
rubrics_metrics.description: Particular incidents either "long command the Attention, or strike with the Violence of a sudden Passion, or occasion the burst of Laughter which accompanies Humour."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Design scenes or particulars to do one (or more) of these: sustain prolonged interest (developing suspense or curiosity), deliver intense emotional impact (sudden passion), or trigger genuine laughter (humour). These kinds of particulars are what keep a story memorable beyond mere elegance of style.

rubrics_metrics.name: Simplicity and naturalness in fable
rubrics_metrics.description: The Arabian fable is praised for "such a wild, but natural Simplicity."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When using fable or parable, favour a simple, natural presentation of events and characters. Avoid overcomplicating the allegory; the pleasing, readable quality of a fable often lies in its straightforward, almost spontaneous telling.

rubrics_metrics.name: Explicit moral or lesson
rubrics_metrics.description: Stories or fables should convey a moral: "I think it has a Moral in it."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If the tale is didactic (as many fables are), ensure the moral is clear — either stated or unmistakably illustrated by the events — so the reader can connect the narrative example to the broader precept being taught.

rubrics_metrics.name: Brevity / contraction of long material
rubrics_metrics.description: "I know you hate long things; but if you like it, you may contract it..."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Be willing to shorten or tighten a narrative. Longness can dull effect; trim excess to keep the reader's attention and leave stronger impact from the key incidents or the moral.

rubrics_metrics.name: Truthful complexity in representing human nature
rubrics_metrics.description: Avoid leveling the best of mankind with the worst; make readers "sensible of both" their greatness and meanness (Pascal's reflection).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Portray characters with both virtues and faults rather than caricaturing all people as entirely good or evil. Balanced depiction sustains moral seriousness and preserves readers' reverence and sympathy, which supports the didactic aims of many essays and fables.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of well-chosen exempla and authoritative references
rubrics_metrics.description: The essay borrows exemplary passages (e.g., Cato, Cyrus, Pascal) to illustrate moral points.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Support abstract reflections with concrete anecdotes, classical examples, or admired authorities to strengthen persuasion and make the point more vivid. Exempla should be relevant and well-integrated into the narrative or essay.
